title: Read distributions and states over time (preview)

blocks.content: Explore four panels on Grafana Play to see the question each one answers.
Explore a histogram to see how its bars group values into numeric ranges, not named categories.

blocks.title: Read a bucket and its count

blocks.content: Open **Histogram Examples**.
Find **Random Timeseries Data**. The histograms on this dashboard reuse its numeric values.
Focus on **Time series + Auto buckets**.

This panel answers the question: How many values fall between 0 and 100, between 100 and 200, and so on? Here the ranges are set automatically from the data. The horizontal axis is the value range, split into buckets, and the vertical axis is the count of values in each bucket. Hover over a bar to read its bucket and count.

Compare a taller bar with a shorter one. The taller bar contains more values in its range. It doesn't necessarily contain the largest values. Position along the horizontal axis identifies the value range.

Unlike the library bar chart, its bars group numbers into ranges rather than named categories. It summarizes the selected observations without showing when each one occurred.
Explore a heatmap to see how each cell combines a time bucket, a numeric range, and a count.
Open **Grafana Heatmaps**.
Find the **Linear** heatmap.

This panel answers the question: How many values fall in each range, and how does that change over time? Time runs along the horizontal axis and numeric value ranges up the vertical axis. Color encodes the count in each cell, so a cell's vertical position isn't its count.
Use the color legend to see which colors mean higher counts, and hover over a cell to read its time, value bucket, and count.

Follow a band of occupied cells from an earlier time to a later time. Notice whether the observations stay in similar value ranges or move higher or lower. This adds the timing that a single histogram leaves out.
Read the legend rather than assuming darker or redder always means more. These are numeric buckets, not healthy or unhealthy states.
Explore a state timeline and a status history to see how one merges equal states into spans and the other keeps each observation separate.
Open **State timeline and Status history**.
Find **State timeline strings**.
This panel answers the question: What state has something been in, and when did it change? Each row is an entity, such as **Level A**, and the horizontal axis is time.

Follow **Level A** from left to right and read states such as LOW, HIGH, and NORMAL. Hover over a NORMAL region to read its time span. Region width represents duration rather than a numeric magnitude.
This example merges consecutive equal values into a continuous region. Read the state label. Color by itself doesn't define its meaning.
State data is formatted as a table with timestamps, an entity name, and a state value. The state can be a string, a number, or a boolean.
Focus on **Status history - boolean values**.

This panel answers the same question as the state timeline, one observation at a time. Each row is a sensor, such as **SensorA**, and each box is one observation. Hover over a box to read its boolean value and timestamp. What true and false mean depends on the sensor. True doesn't always mean healthy.

Adjacent boxes with the same value stay separate. Status history doesn't merge equal consecutive observations into one region the way a state timeline does.
